concepts.title: What is scheduled?
concepts.text: A scheduled job starts a command when its calendar fields match. The supplied virtual UTC clock moves only when you choose Run; it never changes your computer’s clock.

concepts.title: Read the five calendar fields
concepts.text: Read minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week from left to right, followed by the command. Minutes run from 0–59 and hours from 0–23. A star means any value in that field. For weekdays, 1 is Monday through 6 for Saturday; 0 or 7 is Sunday. MON-FRI or 1-5 selects Monday–Friday.

concepts.title: Draft, installed table and output
concepts.text: Type into the table editor, use Install, then choose the end of the virtual interval and Run. A user table runs as its owner and has no username column. The output viewer shows supplied simulated files, not host files.

scenarios.explanation: A declaration before the entries gives LABEL a value in both jobs. LOGNAME comes from the actual job owner. Cron removes the backslash before each escaped percent, then printf uses %s for text and backslash-n for the newline. Appending both the label and current input preserves the existing report. concepts.title: A scheduled environment
concepts.text: A scheduled job does not inherit variables from an interactive terminal. Put ordinary values explicitly in the table before the entries that use them. Declarations are literal and affect following entries.

concepts.title: Supplied and created variables
concepts.text: LOGNAME and USER are supplied from the job’s actual virtual owner; HOME=/work and SHELL=/bin/sh are fixed in this subset. LABEL is a value the learner controls in this table. Double quotes keep each expanded value together.

concepts.title: Two kinds of formatting
concepts.text: printf uses %s for each text argument and backslash-n for a newline. Cron processes percent first, even inside shell quotes: escape each percent as backslash-percent in a table. Unescaped percent input is unsupported and clearly rejected here.

concepts.title: Append preserves earlier output
concepts.text: A single > replaces a file. >> appends to it. Separate jobs at the same minute run in listed order in this simulator; real cron concurrency is not modeled.

concepts.title: Managing a table is different from running it
concepts.text: An access file controls who may install, list or remove user tables. It does not disable a table already installed. Explicitly removing the retired table is a separate task.

concepts.title: Allow file takes precedence
concepts.text: If cron.allow exists, only its listed ordinary users may manage their own tables. cron.deny is considered only when the allow file is absent. An empty allow file allows no ordinary users; a missing allow file is different.

concepts.title: Supplied administrator and owners
concepts.text: The simulated root account can manage supplied tables and access files. A regular account may manage only its own table when policy allows. These are virtual accounts, not credentials or permissions on your computer.

concepts.title: Prove the handover
concepts.text: Run the requested window, inspect the actual owners and output, and check fresh cases. Retain the active owner and peer jobs instead of disabling scheduling for everyone.

scenarios.objective: Publish /work/source to /work/report as reporter at 06:00 on the first day of a month OR on Mondays. Use one system-table entry, remove reporter’s obsolete duplicate user table, and let reporter manage a future user table. Preserve Pat’s table and the peer note. scenarios.explanation: The system table adds reporter as the job owner after its five calendar fields. Restricting both day of month to 1 and weekday to Monday starts on either kind of day; a date matching both still starts one entry once. Removing the obsolete user table prevents a duplicate dispatch. Access policy separately permits future management, while fresh quiet-date, runtime-owner and file-input cases verify the full handover.
hints: Use the system format: five calendar fields, supplied runtime username, then command. A user table does not have that extra username field.
The two restricted day fields use OR; a leading star changes that rule. Test first-of-month, Monday and quiet dates.
Retire the obsolete user table as a separate action, preserve Pat, and allow reporter future management. One successful report alone does not detect duplicates.

cron_teaching.prerequisite_note: Start here if scheduling is new. The linked prerequisite labs teach file commands, redirection and account ownership before this assignment. You may skip or reopen this introduction.

concepts.title: User and system table formats
concepts.text: A user table has five calendar fields and its command; the owner is implicit. A system table adds an explicit supplied username between the fields and command. That account is the job’s runtime identity.

concepts.title: Read the two day fields carefully
concepts.text: When both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, Cronie starts on either matching day. A first-of-month that is also Monday still starts the one entry once. If either day field begins with a star, both day tests must match.

concepts.title: Do not replace a star with a numeric list casually
concepts.text: The original leading star matters to Cronie’s day rule. A full day-number range can select the same numbers as a star but produce a different OR/AND rule when paired with a restricted weekday.

concepts.title: Retire duplicates and verify the complete result
concepts.text: A system entry and a user entry are separate jobs even when their commands are identical. Remove the obsolete user table, retain peer work and check positive and quiet dates with varied supplied inputs.
